text_summary.body: On 24 Shebat of Darius's second year Zechariah saw (1) a man on a red horse among myrtles with a patrol reporting the earth at rest, and heard the angel of the LORD plead for Jerusalem after "these seventy years" and the LORD promise to return with mercy and rebuild; (2) four horns that scattered Judah and four craftsmen to cast them down; (3) a man measuring Jerusalem, told that it would be unwalled for its multitude with the LORD as a wall of fire. An oracle calls the exiles to flee Babylon and promises the LORD's dwelling in Zion and the joining of many nations.

setting.body: Mitchell dates 24 Shebat of Darius's second year to February 519. He doubts that the report "the whole earth rests" describes the empire at that date, given the revolts against Darius, and reads it otherwise.

constraints.textual_assertion: On the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month, which is the month Shebat, in the second year of Darius
assumptions: Babylonian Nisan-based regnal years: year 2 = 3 April 520 – 22 March 519 (Parker & Dubberstein). Shebat (month XI) fell in January–February 519; Mitchell gives "toward the middle of February" 519.

locations.role: "The daughter of Babylon" from which the exiles must flee (2:7)

terminology.term: the angel who talked with me
terminology.gloss: The interpreting angel of the night visions, distinct in the text from the angel of the LORD (1:9, 11–12).

competing_reconstructions.label: "These seventy years" (1:12): from the destruction of 587/586 to Darius's second year
proponents: C. F. Keil (1868), after Vitringa and Hengstenberg: the seventy years were "completed twice"
competing_reconstructions.summary: Jeremiah's seventy years had ended under Cyrus, but nearly seventy years had also passed since the Temple's destruction while it still lay in ruins.

competing_reconstructions.label: "These seventy years" counted from 605 or loosely
competing_reconstructions.summary: Either from the date of Jeremiah's prophecy (605) or by inadvertently including the years since the fall of Babylon.

competing_reconstructions.label: The man among the myrtles
proponents: D. Guzik: the Angel of the LORD, a pre-incarnate appearance of Christ
C. F. Keil: the angel of Jehovah, of one essence with Jehovah
competing_reconstructions.summary: Theological identifications; the text calls him the angel of the LORD (1:11).

commentary.paraphrase: Guzik reads the horsemen as an imperial-style patrol and the horns, if read prophetically, as Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece and Rome.
Guzik sees a short-term fulfilment of 2:1–5 under Ezra and Nehemiah and an ultimate one under the Messiah.
